Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

This lesson is for a drummer who can already play a basic beat: the bass drum on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4, and something steady on top. It is about the “something on top”, and about everything the hi-hat can do besides keeping time. You need a hi-hat with a pedal, a snare and a bass drum. Each step is a little harder than the one before; stay on a step until you can play it through the whole chorus without watching your hands.

How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the groove written large and the whole chorus on a drum staff. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the note that is sounding lights up in the notation. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. The straight steps are played over four bars of F7 by the Straight-eighth rock or Acoustic strum band, and the swing steps over the 12-bar blues by the Swing band. Each step starts at its own tempo; the strip at the bottom changes the tempo, and the Feel menu changes the band. If you cannot yet play a step at its tempo, slow it down until you can.

0. The three sounds of the hi-hat

The hi-hat is two cymbals on a stand, one above the other, with a pedal that opens and closes them. That gives it three sounds you will use all through this lesson.

  • Closed, with the stick. The pedal is down, the cymbals are together, and you hit the top one. A short, tight “tick”. This is the hi-hat sound you hear in most rock.
  • Open, with the stick. You let the pedal up a little, so the cymbals are apart, and hit. The sound rings and hisses until something stops it.
  • Closed, with the foot. You press the pedal and the cymbals come together on their own, with no stick. A soft “chick”.

Click a button to hear each one, and the last button to hear an open note being closed.

Here is how each is written. All three are an ✕, because they are cymbals. A closed note sits above the staff. An open note is the same ✕ with a small circle over it. A note played with the foot is an ✕ below the staff, and its stem points down like the bass drum’s. Click a head to hear it.

The foot closes the cymbals, and that stops an open note. When the cymbals come together, whatever was ringing ends. So an open hi-hat rings until the next closed note or the next foot note cuts it off, whichever comes first. On this page the band’s drummer does the same: press “Open, then the foot” and listen to the open note stop dead. Hearing where an open note ends is as important as hearing where it starts.

1. Quarter notes on the closed hi-hat

The plainest rock beat. The closed hi-hat plays all four beats, the bass drum plays on 1 and 3, and the snare plays on 2 and 4. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” out loud and make the hi-hat as even as the clock.

Two things at once, then three. Start with the hi-hat and the snare alone; add the bass drum when the hands are steady. The hi-hat does not slow down when the snare lands.

2. Eighth notes: the basic rock beat

Now the hi-hat plays twice as often, eight notes to the bar. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. The notes on the numbers fall with the bass drum and the snare; the notes on the “ands” fall in between. The bass drum is still on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4.

Keep the right hand moving in one smooth, even stroke, down on the beat and down on the “and”, and let the snare and the bass drum fit themselves around it.

3. Accents

The same eighth notes, but now they are not all the same. Lean on the notes that fall on the beats and play the “ands” lightly. The usual way to get this is to hit the beats with the shoulder of the stick, on the edge of the hi-hat, and the “ands” with the tip, on top of it; the beats come out louder and brighter, the “ands” softer. The groove starts to breathe.

In the notation, an accent mark (>) is written over each note that is meant to be louder than its neighbours. Look for the mark over the beats in the staff below; the “ands” have none.

Listen with Drums alone. Then play it on a practice pad and try making the difference between the two kinds of note smaller and larger.

4. The off-beats alone

Take the hi-hat off the beats and play it only on the “ands”: and of 1, and of 2, and of 3, and of 4. The bass drum plays on every beat, and the snare is still on 2 and 4. The beats are now played by the feet and the left hand, and the right hand plays in the gaps.

Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud, and tap your foot on the numbers. The hi-hat sits on the words you say between the taps.

5. Opening the hi-hat

Go back to the eighth notes of step 2, and open the hi-hat once: on the and of 4, the last note of the bar. Open it as you hit, let it ring through the end of the bar, and close it on the 1 of the next bar, with the stick and the foot together. Because the cymbals come together, the open note stops right where beat 1 starts.

The open note is written with the small circle. The foot note under the staff, on beat 1 of each bar, is the pedal closing the cymbals. Play it once with the stick alone and once with the foot as well, and listen for the difference.

6. Open on every off-beat: four on the floor

The groove of a dance floor. The bass drum plays on every beat, the snare on 2 and 4, and the hi-hat plays closed on the beats and open on every “and”. Each closed note on the next beat shuts the open one before it, so you hear a “tss-tick, tss-tick” pattern. Your foot has to lift the pedal for each “and” and press it down again for each beat.

This is the same groove as “Four on the floor” in the Drums menu of the Backing Track, with the clap taken off so that you can hear the hi-hat by itself.

7. Sixteenth notes with one hand

At a slow tempo the hi-hat can play four notes to every beat: sixteenths. Count “1 e and a 2 e and a 3 e and a 4 e and a”. One hand plays them all, sixteen to the bar. Play the beats a little stronger than the rest. The bass drum is on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4.

Start very slowly. A slow tempo is the whole point of this step: you are learning to keep sixteen even notes going while the other hand and both feet do something else. Speed up by a few beats a minute at a time.

8. Sixteenth notes with two hands

Now use both hands on the hi-hat, right, left, right, left on the four notes of a beat. Both hands play on the hi-hat. On beats 2 and 4 the right hand has a different job: it comes off the hi-hat to play the snare. So the hi-hat is silent on those two notes, and you play fourteen hi-hat notes to the bar instead of sixteen.

The gap in the hi-hat on 2 and 4 is where the snare sits. Listen for it: the left hand keeps the sixteenths going without a break, and the snare lands in the space the right hand leaves.

9. The foot alone

Now the hi-hat’s foot, which keeps time in a different way. First the jazz setting: time is played on the ride cymbal, and the hi-hat foot closes the cymbals on 2 and 4. The foot is the “chick” that goes with the ride pattern.

Next, a rock beat played on the ride cymbal, with eighth notes on the ride, the bass drum on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4, and the foot closing the hi-hat on all four beats. The right hand is on the ride cymbal, so the hi-hat is played by the foot alone. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” with your foot first, then add the rest.

10. The swing hi-hat

The ride pattern of swing time, played on the hi-hat itself. The pattern is the same as on the ride: a note on each beat, with a skip note after beats 2 and 4. The cymbals are open on 1 and 3, so they ring, and closed on 2 and 4, where the foot closes them with the stick. The skip notes after 2 and 4 are closed. The eighths are swung: the first is long and the second short.

The foot notes on 2 and 4 under the staff are what stop the open notes, and so make the “tss-chick” of swing time. Listen with Drums alone, and notice where the open notes end.

Where to go next

  • Play step 2 or 3 with the drums left out and keep the form of the vamp for ten choruses.
  • For the beat that goes with the 12-bar blues, the ride pattern and the shuffle, go to Blues for Drums.
  • Tools → Backing Track has every groove on this page in its Drums menu, under the names that start “Hi-hat”. The Cymbal menu has “Closed hi-hat”, which puts the hi-hat in place of the ride in the other grooves.
